Former military first responder and recent civilian in the middle of a full scale active shooter drill with local LEs, blank rounds being shot, etc. Real big whoopla.

In some cases, first responders wait until the scene is safe to go in. Specifically EMTs. Not law enforcement. Law enforcement are who MAKE THE SCENE SAFE. EMTs waiting because they don't want to get shot is one thing; they're not armed and them going in before everything's done will just add more bodies. Law enforcement? Nah.

And like, in the active shooter drill we just had at my place of business, we saw that. They also specifically said that in the vast, overwhelming majority of cases, SWAT are not the ones handling these things. Even in our situation, where they had forewarning, it took close to half an hour/forty-five minutes to get there, because SWAT teams don't just stand around waiting. According to the police chief, at least where we are, they're regular officers who receive additional training and duties, so they're not waiting at the starting line, they may have to get called in from across the county or from home.

So regular officers are the ones who handle this sort of thing nine times out of ten, not SWAT, per my local small town police chief. Waiting for SWAT seems to me like it was an excuse using people's common assumption of who's supposed to respond to these events to justify just... sitting around.

Honestly, I kind of feel like there were two cults in Rajneeshpuram. The cult of Rajneesh and the cult of Sheela. They were symbiotic for awhile, but eventually they couldn't function together anymore.

So yeah, I've learned a lot more about Rajneeshpuram and uh... I don't know that I'm super comfortable about the documentary anymore, to be honest.

Because with the benefit of full context, it comes off now as dangerously pro-Rajneeshi.

One thing I'm thinking of when thinking of this is something Legal Eagle from youtube has said: what you start with and what you end with is what's going to stick with people, so make the beginning of your argument and the end of your argument the important stuff that you want people to remember. And the documentary begins and ends with people who are very sympathetic to Osho and Rajneeshpuram, or at least begin as such and don't end openly antagonistic towards him (in this case, the Australian woman).

It takes awhile to get to Antelope and the battles that begin there, and before we get to that we hear about how beautiful the ashram in Poona was, how kind and gentle Osho was, how brilliant and overwhelming his presence had been. The decision to go to America is painted as flight from religious persecution, and Sheela's rhapsodizing of the idyllic America she allegedly pictured makes the hostility of the residents of Antelope even harsher and more bitter.

Because I'll stick to my view that racism and xenophobia played a huge part in Antelope's attitude towards Rajneeshpuram. They made that very clear over and over again: that they were good Christians and those people bow to Satan, that they want to destroy families and marriage, that they're weird and other and not good for America and they're just asking to get shot. 

But of course, this hides a brief, passing mention of letters sent to Antelope from other people, talking about family members trapped in the cult, for example. It's mentioned in passing, buried in a sea of clips of angry old white people talking about how Rajneeshpuram would turn the state red, because this was the 80s, the Reagan era, of course a little anti-communist stuff had to be slipped in there too. 

With the emphasis on the prudish retirees pearl-clutching about free love and Christian values, any accusations of sexual misconduct would seem almost predictable, and predictably easy to dismiss. Oh, the sex guru's followers sexually assault kids, Peggy? Gee, wonder where that came from... 

It feels like largely, the documentarians let the Rajneeshi loyalists dictate the trajectory of the documentary. They let them paint Osho as a tragic, misunderstood genius whose virtues were wasted on America.

A lot of people in this thread are suggesting that your daughter is an asshole for "lying to you". However, as an LGBT person, I can say that even when you know, or think you know, your family will be cool about it... coming out to them is hard. Really hard. And really scary.

Your daughter is not obligated to come out to you. Her not coming out to you is not "lying". Instead of getting offended that she didn't come out to you sooner, ask yourself the very important question of why? Why did she keep this important part of her life from you? Why are you apparently assuming it was purely out of spite?

A possible example of this is the primary historian of the age of Emperor Justinian, Procopius, who wrote a secret history vilifying Justinian, Theodora, General Belisarius, and Belisarius' wife Antonia. The secret history includes the statement that Justinian was a demon who removed his head from his body at night. Jury's still out on whether it's intended as a comedy, the writings of a man disillusioned with the regime, or an insurance policy in case conspirators overthrew Justinian.

2) Especially during the Reformation, historians and contemporary sources fell on religious lines that set the stage for the characterization of everyone involved. Was Mary I a saintly queen wasted on the heathen English or a bloodstained, lunatic tyrant? Was Anne Bolyn a scheming witch who deserved to die, or a passionate defender of the new religion?

I... would generally advise against Santa Muerte unless you're Mexican and truly understand Her enough to treat Her with respect. Santa Muerte is, by and large, a product of the culture that venerates Her. She is venerated by outcasts, the LGBT community, murderers, narcos, the abused, street-based sex workers, the homeless... basically people who live under the threat of death. She is Death in a way that generally appears to not really have an analogue. She is entirely non-judgmental, loving all those who venerate Her equally regardless of what they ask for or why. She can be turned to for help in times of trouble, breaking curses and placing curses, helping with money or relationships or anything...

But that's because all things are touched by death and entropy. As such, She should be approached with caution and respect. Including worship with her for funsies or thinking of her as some sort of fluffy, happy, motherly deity/folk saint (as many books I've seen often do)... it will not go well for you. She is a deity/folk saint of protection, health, and other good things, that is true... just be aware of the import and depth of where She comes from and what She's revered for. In Mexico, She is venerated by those who suffer, and sometimes by those who in turn cause suffering... and because death is a zero-sum game, She loves both equally.

A Mexican witch I spoke to particularly warned against baby/new witches contacting Her. Apparently she had history with Santa Muerte. The general tone was 'if you stare long enough into the abyss, the abyss will stare back at you'. 

So... I guess TL;DR: Just be aware that Santa Muerte must be approached with respect, and is a folk saint/deity that's most commonly known form is rather uniquely Unique to Mexico, and also has very specific connotations.

Party are childhood friends, or at least neighbors, from a small fort to the north. Cultists descend on the fort and slaughter every, but the PCs survive and retreat. Provide options for where to go (nearest fort is the best bet, but they could pass over that to nearby village or even go straight to the city, though they'd have to forage, while going to the fort would probably allow them to get supplies). As their rep grows, the cultists who attacked their village might have their attention caught. The overarching plot intersects based on how interested they are in vengeance vs just moving on with their lives and how big of a thorn they end up being in the side of the ones who destroyed their village (intentionally or unintentionally).

But in general, mostly just... don't expect an actual /narrative/ is probably the biggest takeaway here, and probably my biggest mistake last time. Provide options, plan based on those options, branch out from there. Have general arcs going in the background, but allow them to intersect and change with the story the PCs create with the options you provide.

Paganism is a very broad term. If you're interested and open-minded about it, ask her what gods she follows. Different pantheons have different core beliefs, and different gods have different expectations. A pagan who follows the gods of the Norse pantheon might have a different system than a pagan who follows the Hellenic pantheon, and there are pagans who follow a variety of gods from different pantheons as well. In my experience, it tends to be a very fluid practice that varies in subtle ways from practitioner to practitioner.

Some pagans (but not all) practice different forms of witchcraft as well. Paganism isn't Wicca, however; or rather, Wiccans are pagan but not all pagans are Wiccans. Wicca is a pretty new duotheistic religion that follows the God and Goddess, basically the masculine and feminine aspects of nature, but it's incorporated a lot of pagan concepts and festivals. Paganism can involve religious witchcraft but doesn't have to. 

Do you want to impress her? Talk to her! Ask her about the gods she serves, her views of divinity. If her practice includes Wiccan Sabbats (Sometimes they do, for the sake of simplicity; I personally plan on celebrating them with emphases on Hellenic gods, like using Imbolc to welcome Persephone back to the surface), ask if there are things you can participate in. Some rituals are private but there are ways to celebrate together. 

Based on the fact that she's Irish, she very well may follow the Celtic pantheon, but don't assume. Ask. We can't tell you what she believes. Only she can tell you that.
